summary: The note explains how confit, the traditional French preservation technique of slow-cooking food submerged in fat, oil, or syrup, can be adapted to be more sustainable. It covers ethical and local ingredient sourcing, substituting fats such as olive oil for duck fat, reducing energy use with efficient appliances, reusing leftover fats, home-cooking approaches, and educational outreach by chefs and experts.
one_line: Confit, the traditional French preservation technique, can be made eco-friendly through responsible sourcing, fat substitution, energy-efficient cooking, waste reduction, and education.
key_facts: Confit comes from the French word "confire," which roughly translates to "to preserve."
Duck confit (confit de canard) dates back to the 17th Century, though the method itself is older.
Confit traditionally involves slow-cooking food in grease, oils, or syrups at temperatures well below frying, often around 90°C (194°F).
Food is totally submerged in fat or sugar-containing substance, creating an anaerobic cooking environment that prevents spoilage.
On September 5, 2023, at the Sustainable Cooking Symposium in Lyons, chef Henri Dubois said confit techniques arose out of necessity to preserve foods before refrigerators or freezers existed.

On November 16, 2023, at the Eco-Culinaire conference in Montreal, Michelin-starred chef Alessandra Patelli showed duck fat could be substituted with olive oil infused with herbs for a more sustainable twist.
Food activist Michael Richardson said at "Eco-Kitchen Talks" on September 20, 2023, in San Francisco that "The ethical dimension of our ingredients is as pivotal as the culinary technique we choose."
Richardson argues local, seasonal sourcing guarantees freshness and reduces the carbon footprint of transporting goods.
On October 14, 2023, Dr. Emily Saunders said a well-insulated electric slow cooker or pressure cooker can significantly reduce energy consumption compared to traditional oven methods.
Residual fats and oils from confit can be strained, stored, and reused several times, limiting waste and honoring the 'nose-to-tail' philosophy.
Julie Thompson published a home-cook guide on her website 'EcoEats' on September 12, 2023, recommending less common cuts of meat and smaller, tightly packed cooking vessels to use less oil.

Chef Giovanni Ferro held a sustainable cooking workshop at the University of Gastronomic Sciences in Polenzo, Italy, on December 2, 2023, teaching traditional methods like confit with sustainable adaptations.
